extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patentees, inventors, and legal students studying patent law (UK/common-law context)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for assessing and obtaining patents under common-law/UK practice, focused on what kinds of inventions are protectable and the legal incidents of utility and novelty (including true-inventor and public-use doctrines). Useful for advising patentees or litigating validity/infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: A new combination of old parts may be patentable provided some degree of invention has been manifested in arriving at the new combination or process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and discussion: Ransell v. Cowley (manufacture of tubes without a mandrel) — the new process produced longer, more uniform, and cheaper tubes; combinations that include some inventive step in arranging old components can be valid. If one part of a combination is new (even minor), the whole combination may be considered new.

rubrics_metrics.name: New part makes whole combination new
rubrics_metrics.description: If any one of the parts of a combination is new, it follows that the entire combination is new too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as a principle: introduction of a new component within an otherwise old combination confers novelty on the combination as a whole (see accompanying examples in text).

rubrics_metrics.name: New shape or configuration of an old element
rubrics_metrics.description: The introduction into an old combination of a new shape of one of the old elements, which new shape invokes a physical law otherwise left on one side (e.g., employing a filament of carbon instead of a thick rod in an incandescent lamp), is a good subject for a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Edison (carbon filament) cited. The novelty can arise from a change in form that produces a new physical effect or utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: New mode of applying a known thing
rubrics_metrics.description: A new mode of applying a thing may be the subject of a patent, provided that some ingenuity, some novelty, is exhibited in the mode of making that application, and that the application is attended by some useful result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Watt's patent for enclosing cylinder to lessen steam consumption; Forsyth's patent for using known fulminating compounds to discharge firearms — courts held these novel applications patentable when the application itself was new and useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture defined as vendible article produced by hand/art
rubrics_metrics.description: A manufacture is a vendible article produced by the hand and art of man; even where materials are old, a new combination or new result can be a manufacture and thus patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Cornish v. Keene — use of india-rubber threads combined with filamentous materials produced a new cloth; court emphasized that new result/production counts as manufacture even if constituent materials were known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of mechanical process/apparatus improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: An improved mode and apparatus for performing a known operation may be patentable if it produces a new, useful result (even where heat or other known techniques are applied in a new context).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: apparatus for bending wood handles using heat and mandrel (Dangerfield v. Jones) — court refused to accept argument that applying a known operation in a new context is not patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical processes and industrial scaling
rubrics_metrics.description: Chemical processes (sometimes with mechanical contrivances) that produce or effect something useful are patentable; producing a substance in small laboratory quantities previously does not preclude a patent for a method allowing large-scale, merchantable production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: distillation of bituminous minerals, purification of coal gas, preparation of dyes, electro-deposition of nickel, manufacture of alum. Case: Young v. Fernie — inventing an industrially practical method for a substance previously only a laboratory curiosity supports a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility (general requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility is an essential incident of every invention claiming patent protection; if a head of invention is useless the patent is void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: Morgan v. Seward, Simpson v. Holliday, Templeton v. Macfarlane. A patent for a useless invention is void because monopolies in useless inventions harm trade and public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent must not be merely to obstruct improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent for an invention which is merely to obstruct every subsequent improvement, to prevent the exercise of the ingenuity of mankind and introduction of other inventions, cannot be supported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chief Baron Pollock's observation: patents obtained solely to block improvements (not to introduce a useful invention) are fraudulent and void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility measured against prior trade knowledge (not abstract utility)
rubrics_metrics.description: In patent law utility means an invention better than the preceding knowledge of the trade as to a particular fabric; it does not mean abstract utility. Any new point of utility not present before suffices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted guidance (Mr Justice Grove): if any new point of utility is present which was not in previous known things, it is useful; but if it's no better in any particular point, it is not useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantum of utility: slightest benefit suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: The quantum of improvement is not material; the slightest amount of utility is sufficient to sustain a patent. In jury trials they decide utility or no utility, not the extent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Philpot v. Hanbury; Neilson v. Harford — juries consider whether invention is of any use at all; even very small utility will do, provided it is evidence-based.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility must reside in the invention, not merely the product
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the invention which must possess utility, not merely the thing produced; the invention must effect the utility (e.g., be better in quality or cheaper in cost than what it replaces).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pollock, C.B.: proving the produced article is useful is not sufficient; the inventive step itself must be responsible for the utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger in the only described mode can vitiate patent
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention as put into practice in the only way described in the specification is not only useless but dangerous, the patent is fatally objectionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Easterbrook v. Great Western Railway Co. — specification that leads to dangerous practice can render the patent invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of utility: commercial success and working
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial sale or extensive market acceptance shortly after first manufacture is proof (and cogent evidence) of utility and may also bear on novelty, but commercial success is not necessary to establish utility; utility must be judged as at the date of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: American Braided Wire Co. v. Thomson; Badische Anilin und Soda Fabrik v. Levinstein — courts warn that commercial success is relevant but not conclusive; later obsolescence does not invalidate a patent that was useful at filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-working is prima facie evidence against utility but not conclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention is not worked by the inventor, that fact is prima facie evidence of want of utility; however, subsequent improvements or sales of improved versions do not necessarily show the original invention was useless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law shows courts accept evidence (e.g., witnesses that an invention will work) and that not selling the original form is not decisive if there's evidence of utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial uselessness and essentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: The uselessness of part of an invention will not vitiate the whole patent unless that part is described as something essential to the invention (or unless its inclusion misleads the public).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lewis v. Marling: where a brush claimed was later found unnecessary but not described as essential, the patent was not held void; if patentee knowingly includes a useless 'essential' element to mislead, the patent may be invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (general requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention is destitute of novelty the patent is void; moreover, if several distinct heads of invention are claimed and one is old, that will invalidate the whole patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute of James and case law: Morgan v. Seward, Hill v. Thompson, Brunton v. Hawkes — the Crown's grant is based on novelty of what is claimed; deception as to extent invalidates entire grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two novelty questions: true inventor and prior public knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty queries whether (1) the patentee was the true inventor and (2) whether the invention was new to the public at its date (including whether it had been in public use, described in printed book, earlier specification, or prior publication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text enumerates modes by which prior public knowledge defeats novelty: public use, printed descriptions accessible to the public, earlier specifications, prior publications by inventor or others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public possession/public use defeats novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: When the public has become possessed of an invention in any manner whatever before the patent date, no valid patent for it can subsequently be obtained (with certain exceptions discussed elsewhere).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look to whether invention had become part of the public stock of knowledge before the patent date; 'public use' is a critical disqualifying factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: True and first inventor requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If it can be shown that the person to whom the patent was granted was not the true and first inventor (e.g., he borrowed it from another), the patent is invalid under the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gibson v. Brand and other authorities: even a perfectly new discovery may not save a patent if obtained from another's labours; conversely, where a prior discoverer kept it private (Dr. Hall in Dollond case), a subsequent patentee who first brought it to public use may be treated as the first inventor for patent purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority between rival inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: If two persons independently make the same invention about the same time, the one who first obtains a patent (or brings it into public use) will usually be treated as the first inventor provided there was no prior public use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Muirlinj, Hill v. Thompson — independent concurrent invention does not deprive a patentee who first patents/uses it publicly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint inventorship and material contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: If an invention results from the combined operation of two or more minds, all of the inventors should apply for the patent; if a patentee owed a material part of the invention to another person, this can be fatal to validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where contributions from others constitute material inventive input, failing to include them can render the patent invalid; contrast with mere workmen's assistance (see next).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assistants/workmen contributions do not necessarily negate inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestions and aid of workmen employed by the inventor will not, by themselves, deprive the inventor of the right to a patent; the substantial part and leading idea/principle must belong to the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alderson J.'s jury directions in Minter v. Wells: distinguish between a workman who carries out an inventor's conception and a true co-inventor; evidence of who suggested the principle and who merely executed is decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imported inventions may be considered 'true and first' inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: An importer of an invention from abroad can be held by the courts to fall within the meaning of 'true and first inventor' for patent purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noted as a caveat in the text: importation of technology from abroad and first local exploitation/patenting can satisfy the 'true and first' requirement in some contexts.
